extraction.body: Three years into tracking consumer AI, the leaderboard is becoming familiar. This is the seventh edition of our Top 100 AI Consumer Apps, where we rank the top web and mobile AI products by monthly traffic. (You can read our previous ones — I , II III , IV , V , VI — to see how these have evolved over time.) Just 11 products make their first-ever appearance in this edition — the smallest number of debuts across our seven lists so far. But traffic data alone increasingly conceals the real trends in consumer AI. For the first time, we’re adding a ranking by observed spending on U.S. consumer cards, thanks to YipitData. This gives us another way to see the market, including dozens of vendors absent from our web and mobile lists — like desktop apps, and agents inside existing messaging platforms. The biggest takeaway from this new data? Consumer AI usage is wide, but not very deep…for almost everyone. While nearly half of U.S. consumers now report using AI, only 25% are engaged with it daily. And as of August, just 4.5% of U.S. consumers had an active paid personal subscription to ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude. You can get more data on broad AI adoption in our State of Markets presentation we shared last week. However, AI’s consumer power users are extremely engaged — and highly monetizable. The top 10% of spenders account for roughly half of all observed spending. These high spenders disproportionately buy coding, productivity, and creative tools. In these users, consumer AI has found its first real market: people who pay — often a lot — for tools that help them build, create, and get work done. Reaching everyone else will likely take different products. We’re seeing glimmers of this now with the launch of personal assistants that, unlike their ancestor OpenClaw, are usable by non-developers — and free. Alongside these product capability improvements, consumer AI likely needs a new business model — or possibly, an old one. Essentially all AI revenue has come from direct subscriptions or usage charges, unlike prior eras where consumers were monetized indirectly via ads or transactional revenue. This has likely been a limiting factor in deeper consumer adoption. As in our previous editions, we rank the top 50 web products by monthly visits, using Similarweb, and the top 50 mobile apps by monthly active users, using Sensor Tower. Generative AI must be central to the product experience; both AI-native companies and established products can qualify. We’re making one change to eligibility from this list forward: products primarily designed for NSFW use cases will be excluded. This should not be interpreted as a decrease in demand for these products — we’re treating them as a distinct category rather than ranking them alongside SFW products. Consumer AI’s headline is the same as our very first report in September 2023 — ChatGPT was the pioneer, and remains the leader. It has a roughly 2x lead on Gemini in August web visits and an even wider lead over Claude (6x). This gap is more significant on mobile, where ChatGPT has a 2.5x lead on Gemini and a 14x lead on Claude in monthly active users. Our new revenue data tells a similar story. Per YipitData’s panel, ChatGPT has 3x more U.S. consumer paid subscribers than Claude or Gemini. The most significant shift in this landscape has been Claude emerging as the clear #3. Claude did not even rank on our first web list in September 2023, but has now passed competitors like DeepSeek and Perplexity in traffic. Even more significantly, Claude passed Gemini on U.S. consumer subscribers earlier this year. Even after Google migrated legacy paid users over to the AI plan (inorganically inflating subscriber count), Gemini and Claude are neck and neck. Claude’s run came on the back of new products (Cowork in January, Claude Design in April), new models (Fable 5 in June), and a burst of public attention. Amid Anthropic’s late-February dispute with the Pentagon, Claude hit #1 among free U.S. mobile apps for the first time. Unlike OpenAI and Google, Anthropic has been clear that they will not run ads in Claude, and instead monetize users via subscription. They have been doing so aggressively. Claude has 7.3% of consumer payers on their most expensive individual plan, Max — which starts at $100/month. This compares to 1.3% for Google and 1.1% for ChatGPT on their corresponding $100/month subscriptions. This difference in users is at least partially a result of the products being pointed in different directions. Between Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, there were 127 new launches over the past six months. Anthropic has focused almost entirely on the prosumer (Claude Design, Code Review, Claude Science ). Google has led on creative models (Lyria 3 Pro, Gemini Omni). OpenAI has tackled both consumer and enterprise — with tools for enterprise (ChatGPT Work, Sites, Dots) and for consumers (Images 2.0, Health, Personal Finance, job search). For the first time, we’re adding a ranking based on observed consumer spending, using data from YipitData. The data is U.S.-only and drawn from panels rather than a census; so it should not be read as total company revenue. However — it gives us a new view of how consumers pay for AI, with a clear takeaway: heavy concentration. The base of consumers paying for AI is growing, but still narrow. In August, 4.5% of eligible consumers in YipitData’s U.S. e-receipt panel had an active paid personal subscription to at least one of ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude, up from 2.1% a year ago. Even among the relatively narrow band of paying consumer users, spending follows a power law. Only 13% of users who pay for one AI product pay for even one other AI tool. And, spend from the top 1% of payers accounted for 19.5% of all observed consumer AI spend. This is more than the bottom 50% of spenders combined (16.6%). This top 1% pays an average of $903 per month on consumer cards for AI (work usage may be even higher), as of August 2026. And, they’re still growing this spend — up 80% in the last 18 months. The difference from the median AI payer is stark: they are spending $25 per month, and barely have expanded this spend over time. We expect the paying base to broaden as business models open up. Personal agents, in particular, show potential to monetize on transactions rather than seats, offering something closer to unlimited usage without a subscription. More on that later in the report. In March, we wrote that agents like OpenClaw were not yet usable by most consumers — but would be. Six months later, multiple startup consumer or prosumer agent products now report hundreds of thousands of users, including Instinct, Tomo, Poke, Lindy, and Town. And, the incumbents have struck back with agents of their own — Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, and xAI’s Grok Bot. Most of these agents strive to be available everywhere — like a human assistant, you can text, email, or call. The channel du jour is iMessage, where viral agent Instinct launched in August 2026. Companies like DoorDash have since launched their own iMessage agent for text-to-order. More prosumer-oriented agents, or consumer agents focused on a specialized use case, often also have their own mobile or web app to provide a deeper experience. As agents start to drive meaningful traffic (and revenue), the platforms are choosing sides . Amazon shut down access for Meta’s Muse in under two weeks, while Shopify, Instacart, OpenTable, Expedia, Ticketmaster, Plaid, and others have signed official integrations. passages: Three years into tracking consumer AI, the leaderboard is becoming familiar. This is the seventh edition of our Top 100 AI Consumer Apps, where we rank the top web and mobile AI products by monthly traffic. (You can read our previous ones — I , II III , IV , V , VI — to see how these have evolved over time.) Just 11 products make their first-ever appearance in this edition — the smallest number of debuts across our seven lists so far.

But traffic data alone increasingly conceals the real trends in consumer AI. For the first time, we’re adding a ranking by observed spending on U.S. consumer cards, thanks to YipitData. This gives us another way to see the market, including dozens of vendors absent from our web and mobile lists — like desktop apps, and agents inside existing messaging platforms.

The biggest takeaway from this new data? Consumer AI usage is wide, but not very deep…for almost everyone. While nearly half of U.S. consumers now report using AI, only 25% are engaged with it daily. And as of August, just 4.5% of U.S. consumers had an active paid personal subscription to ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude. You can get more data on broad AI adoption in our State of Markets presentation we shared last week.

However, AI’s consumer power users are extremely engaged — and highly monetizable. The top 10% of spenders account for roughly half of all observed spending. These high spenders disproportionately buy coding, productivity, and creative tools.

In these users, consumer AI has found its first real market: people who pay — often a lot — for tools that help them build, create, and get work done. Reaching everyone else will likely take different products. We’re seeing glimmers of this now with the launch of personal assistants that, unlike their ancestor OpenClaw, are usable by non-developers — and free.

Essentially all AI revenue has come from direct subscriptions or usage charges, unlike prior eras where consumers were monetized indirectly via ads or transactional revenue. This has likely been a limiting factor in deeper consumer adoption.

As in our previous editions, we rank the top 50 web products by monthly visits, using Similarweb, and the top 50 mobile apps by monthly active users, using Sensor Tower. Generative AI must be central to the product experience; both AI-native companies and established products can qualify.

We’re making one change to eligibility from this list forward: products primarily designed for NSFW use cases will be excluded. This should not be interpreted as a decrease in demand for these products — we’re treating them as a distinct category rather than ranking them alongside SFW products.

It has a roughly 2x lead on Gemini in August web visits and an even wider lead over Claude (6x). extraction.body: Well, the good news is Andreessen Horowitz just released its third installment of Top 100 Gen AI Consumer Apps, which rounds up the most-used apps in the space. It's an excellent way to find some lesser-known apps that are gaining traction — and see how the big players in the space are stacking up against each other. Every six months, the venture capital firm ranks the top 50 AI-first web products by unique monthly visits and the top 50 AI-first mobile apps by monthly active users. Unsurprisingly, OpenAI's ChatGPT remains king, topping both lists for the third time. Apps like Microsoft Edge and Photomath remained in 2nd and 3rd place, respectively, and Character.AI rose from 3rd place to replace Gemini in 2nd for web products. While the AI giants continue to battle it out, some newer rising stars are also making inroads — and getting people creative. Of the 12 new entrants to the list, 58% are creative tools focused on content generation or editing images, videos, music, speech, and more, according to the study. Music generator app Suno — which lets you easily make an AI song based on a text prompt — made the biggest jump for creative tools, rising from 36th to 5th in web products. Newcomer Udio, another generative model that produces songs via text prompts, ranked 33rd. AI-powered dating app RIZZ made the mobile list for the first time, ranking 49th. Aesthetics apps like LooksMax AI and Umax were also new entrants, ranking 43rd and 44th, respectively. You can see the full list Andreessen Horowitz's website.

sources.title: Pakistan security forces adopt fishing nets to counter low-cost terrorist drone attacks - streamlinefeed.co.ke
passages: In the rugged, sensitive terrains of northern Pakistan, security forces and local police are deploying an unconventional, low-cost defensive measure to counter a modern and lethal threat: reinforced fishing nets strung high above security outposts and government buildings.

The initiative, primarily concentrated in the province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, represents a pragmatic adaptation of tactics recently observed in Eastern Europe, designed to mitigate the growing use of modified commercial drones by armed militant groups to drop explosives on fortified positions.
Portable, backpack-mounted drone jammers are being issued to patrol units, while larger, fixed anti-drone domes are being installed over critical infrastructure and major bases.

These EW systems work by flooding the frequencies used by commercial drones, severing the link between the pilot and the aircraft, or spoofing GPS signals to force the drone to land or return to its launch point.
The fishing nets, therefore, act as the kinetic backstop for when electronic measures fail or when drones operate in "return-to-home" autonomous modes after losing their signal.
For the Pakistani state, countering this drone threat is a matter of urgent national security.
The psychological impact of constant aerial surveillance and the random nature of drone-dropped explosives severely degrades the morale of security personnel stationed in isolated outposts.
By implementing visible, tangible defensive measures like the overhead nets, commanders aim to restore a sense of security and operational confidence among their troops.
The nets are highly susceptible to larger, faster military-grade unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) or drones equipped with shaped charges designed to defeat physical barriers.
The adoption of these nets underscores the escalating security challenges in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the neighboring border regions.

Following the US withdrawal from Afghanistan and the subsequent resurgence of the Taliban, militant groups such as the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) have significantly ramped up cross-border attacks and internal insurgent operations.
This tactic closely mirrors the widespread use of protective netting and "cages" by both Ukrainian and Russian forces to defend against Iranian-designed Shahed kamikaze drones and FPV strikes.
Recognizing the efficacy of this low-tech solution against high-tech threats, Pakistani security planners have rapidly integrated the nets into their standard operating procedures for static defence.
The physical nets serve as a crucial last line of defence, catching the drones that manage to evade electronic detection or operate autonomously in GPS-denied environments.

Police and security outposts in northern Pakistan are stringing reinforced fishing nets overhead as a low-cost, Ukraine-inspired defence against explosive-laden commercial drones. In the rugged, sensitive terrains of northern Pakistan, security forces and local police are deploying an unconventional, low-cost defensive measure to counter a modern and lethal threat: reinforced fishing nets strung high above security outposts and government buildings. The initiative, primarily concentrated in the province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, represents a pragmatic adaptation of tactics recently observed in Eastern Europe, designed to mitigate the growing use of modified commercial drones by armed militant groups to drop explosives on fortified positions. The proliferation of cheap, commercially available quadcopters and first-person view (FPV) drones has fundamentally altered the tactical landscape of asymmetric warfare and regional terrorism. Militant factions, lacking the resources to acquire sophisticated military-grade aerial munitions, have instead weaponized off-the-shelf technology. By attaching small explosive payloads or mortar rounds to these agile devices, they can bypass traditional perimeter defences, hover over fortified compounds, and release munitions with devastating precision. For the police and paramilitary forces stationed in remote outposts, these buzzing aerial threats have become a persistent and deadly hazard. The countermeasure is remarkably simple in its execution. Strung several metres overhead across the roofs and courtyards of vulnerable installations, the nets act as a physical barrier designed to intercept incoming drones before they can reach their intended targets. Made from extra-durable, bespoke threading, the reinforced mesh is intended to tangle the rotors of the low-flying drones, causing them to crash or lose stability. In many cases, the physical obstruction triggers the drone's payload to detonate prematurely in the air or on the net itself, safely away from the personnel and infrastructure below. This tactic closely mirrors the widespread use of protective netting and "cages" by both Ukrainian and Russian forces to defend against Iranian-designed Shahed kamikaze drones and FPV strikes. Recognizing the efficacy of this low-tech solution against high-tech threats, Pakistani security planners have rapidly integrated the nets into their standard operating procedures for static defence. The materials are inexpensive, locally sourced, and can be rapidly deployed over existing structures without requiring complex engineering or heavy logistical support. While the fishing nets have proven effective against small, slow-moving commercial drones dropping lightweight explosives, security analysts caution that they are not a panacea for the broader aerial threat. The nets are highly susceptible to larger, faster military-grade unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) or drones equipped with shaped charges designed to defeat physical barriers. Furthermore, militants can adapt by flying at higher altitudes before dropping payloads, or by using heavier munitions that can easily tear through the mesh netting upon impact. Consequently, the nets are viewed as part of a layered defence strategy rather than a standalone solution. They are most effective when combined with electronic warfare capabilities, such as localized drone jammers that sever the communication link between the operator and the device, and kinetic interceptors like anti-aircraft machine guns. The physical nets serve as a crucial last line of defence, catching the drones that manage to evade electronic detection or operate autonomously in GPS-denied environments. The adoption of these nets underscores the escalating security challenges in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the neighboring border regions. Following the US withdrawal from Afghanistan and the subsequent resurgence of the Taliban, militant groups such as the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) have significantly ramped up cross-border attacks and internal insurgent operations. The use of drone technology by these groups highlights their increasing tactical sophistication and ability to exploit global supply chains for dual-use technologies. The psychological impact of constant aerial surveillance and the random nature of drone-dropped explosives severely degrades the morale of security personnel stationed in isolated outposts. By implementing visible, tangible defensive measures like the overhead nets, commanders aim to restore a sense of security and operational confidence among their troops. As drone technology continues to evolve and become cheaper, the image of fishing nets guarding military outposts is likely to become a defining visual motif of modern, low-intensity counter-terrorism operations in the region. Insurgents frequently employ modified commercial quadcopters and custom-built, fixed-wing foam drones offering greater range and payload capacity. These devices are often flown at night or during low-light conditions to avoid visual detection. The payloads, while small, are highly lethal in the confined spaces of a security outpost, often consisting of modified mortar shells or commercially available explosives rigged with 3D-printed release mechanisms. The fishing nets, therefore, act as the kinetic backstop for when electronic measures fail or when drones operate in "return-to-home" autonomous modes after losing their signal. extraction.body: Hangu, Pakistan – Police officer Fayyaz Khan and his colleagues ducked for cover as drones carrying explosives rained them down on their checkpost in northwest Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province this year. The April 16 attack was claimed by Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), commonly known as the Pakistan Taliban, and its fighters then opened fire from all sides of the Sarki Piyala police checkpost in Hangu district, about 30km (18 miles) from the border with Afghanistan and a hotbed of deadly attacks by armed groups, mainly the TTP. The confrontation lasted roughly seven hours, killed the driver of an armoured vehicle and injured a constable, Khan, a 40-year-old police inspector, recalled. “There was a great deal of fear because we were in the middle of a battle. At that moment, we did not even know whether we would make it back home alive,” Khan told Al Jazeera. To defend against such attacks, the police in Hangu came up with an unlikely, low-cost solution – fishing nets strung several metres overhead between the checkpost’s rooftops and perimeter walls, forming a kind of aerial ceiling. Simple in construction and resembling what fishermen use for their work, the netting was first installed two months ago, according to the local police. Since then, Khan said, no drone attacks have taken place at Sarki Piyala. “If a drone comes over the checkpoint, there is a possibility that it could get caught in the net and be defused or stopped,” he said as his colleagues, strapped into bullet-resistant vests and holding guns in their hands, kept watch beneath a canopy of black mesh patched together with rope and wire. A standard checkpost can be covered with such nets for about 400,000 Pakistani rupees ($1,435), Hangu district police officer Tariq Habib told Al Jazeera. “The police have introduced the netting system at vulnerable police stations and checkposts to reduce the impact of drone and quadcopter attacks,” Habib said, adding that more nets were being installed at police stations across the district. He said the police in Hangu have asked for additional funding from the provincial government to expand the programme and their request is under review. A spokesman for the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police said the nets have been installed at checkpoints and police posts in at least five other vulnerable districts: Kohat, Karak, Bannu, Lakki Marwat and Dera Ismail Khan. Even military outposts at some sites in the province have deployed the antidrone netting system. The fishing nets have been put up in response to a shift in the tactics of armed groups, which are pairing gunfire and mortars with drones and quadcopters. Pakistan has seen an increase in armed attacks in recent years, mainly targeting the police and the military, with many of them claimed by the TTP, which says it is fighting for a Taliban-style, religious-driven government in Pakistan. Pakistani officials have repeatedly accused Kabul’s Taliban government of providing the TTP a safe haven on its soil and have demanded that it prevent cross-border attacks into Pakistan. Kabul has denied the accusations and called the attacks Islamabad’s domestic security problem. In Hangu, the deadliest of such attacks happened on July 29 when attackers stormed a police outpost with quadcopters rigged with bombs before launching a ground ambush, killing at least 11 police officers and wounding 28. Fifteen attackers were also killed in the hours-long assault, claimed by the TTP. On September 20, another exchange of fire in Hangu killed six soldiers and eight attackers, according to the Pakistani army. That attack came two days after another armed group, called Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, killed 23 people, including 16 police officers, and bombed a mosque in coordinated attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Kohat district. Police said they have recorded at least 16 attacks in Hangu this year, making it one of the most sensitive districts in the province. But police officer Zeeshan Khan said no drone or quadcopter attacks have occurred at Sarki Piyala and the nearby Baliamena checkposts since the fishing nets went up. He said the nets provide “an extra layer of security” to police personnel. “If an attack does take place, the arrangements we have made can reduce the potential damage,” he said, estimating that the measures could reduce potential losses by 40 to 50 percent. The frequent armed attacks have reshaped the daily lives of the people in Hangu who live near the police checkposts. Mohammad Usama, a 28-year-old social activist in Baliamena, said the attacks often prompt families to pull children out of school. “There is always a fear that a stray bullet or something else could hit our children, brothers, cousins,” Usama said. “We just pray that Allah ends terrorism in our country so that we can live peacefully in our area, our children can continue their education and people can go to work without fear.” Usama said since the fishing net was put up in his area, he has noticed a decline in ambushes. But security experts said the strategy may offer a “false sense of security”. “Deploying nets at particular locations is an immature, cheap ploy because police stations are not necessarily always the target,” Imtiaz Gul, executive director of the Islamabad-based Centre for Research and Security Studies, told Al Jazeera. “The drones are intended to hit prominent locations and generate dramatic optics.” “Drones are a source of scare and terror, and they can generate this intended spectacle whenever they are able to hit a strategic, important public location,” he said. Fida Adeel, a Peshawar-based analyst specialising in counterterrorism and security, said the fishing nets are not a new concept. He traced them to camouflage nets used by the military to conceal their equipment. More recently, he said, they were adapted in Ukraine as a way to intercept Russian drones. Adeel cautioned that the effectiveness of a fishing net against explosive-laden drones depends on its design and deployment. He also questioned whether the police estimates of “40 to 50 percent protection” could be verified without real-world trials. “The extent of protection can only be determined through proper testing,” he said. In response, Abdul Salam Khalid, a spokesman for the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police, told Al Jazeera they conducted a formal trial of the netting system in Kohat. He said an explosive was dropped on one of the nets during the trial, but it did not explode. Back in Hangu, police inspector Khan said he knows that having fishing nets over his head is no foolproof solution. For him and his colleagues, he said, the nets offer some reassurance, even if they cannot eliminate the risks they face while on duty. “We cannot say that the netting system provides complete protection,” Khan said.

story.title: Pakistan installs fishing nets at security outposts to block drone attacks - Al Jazeera

facts.text: In the rugged, sensitive terrains of northern Pakistan, security forces and local police are deploying an unconventional, low-cost defensive measure to counter a modern and lethal threat: reinforced fishing nets strung high above security outposts and government buildings.

The initiative, primarily concentrated in the province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, represents a pragmatic adaptation of tactics recently observed in Eastern Europe, designed to mitigate the growing use of modified commercial drones by armed militant groups to drop explosives on fortified positions.
Portable, backpack-mounted drone jammers are being issued to patrol units, while larger, fixed anti-drone domes are being installed over critical infrastructure and major bases.

These EW systems work by flooding the frequencies used by commercial drones, severing the link between the pilot and the aircraft, or spoofing GPS signals to force the drone to land or return to its launch point.
The fishing nets, therefore, act as the kinetic backstop for when electronic measures fail or when drones operate in "return-to-home" autonomous modes after losing their signal.
For the Pakistani state, countering this drone threat is a matter of urgent national security.
The psychological impact of constant aerial surveillance and the random nature of drone-dropped explosives severely degrades the morale of security personnel stationed in isolated outposts.
By implementing visible, tangible defensive measures like the overhead nets, commanders aim to restore a sense of security and operational confidence among their troops.
The nets are highly susceptible to larger, faster military-grade unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) or drones equipped with shaped charges designed to defeat physical barriers.
The adoption of these nets underscores the escalating security challenges in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the neighboring border regions.

Following the US withdrawal from Afghanistan and the subsequent resurgence of the Taliban, militant groups such as the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) have significantly ramped up cross-border attacks and internal insurgent operations.
This tactic closely mirrors the widespread use of protective netting and "cages" by both Ukrainian and Russian forces to defend against Iranian-designed Shahed kamikaze drones and FPV strikes.
Recognizing the efficacy of this low-tech solution against high-tech threats, Pakistani security planners have rapidly integrated the nets into their standard operating procedures for static defence.
The physical nets serve as a crucial last line of defence, catching the drones that manage to evade electronic detection or operate autonomously in GPS-denied environments.

Police and security outposts in northern Pakistan are stringing reinforced fishing nets overhead as a low-cost, Ukraine-inspired defence against explosive-laden commercial drones. In the rugged, sensitive terrains of northern Pakistan, security forces and local police are deploying an unconventional, low-cost defensive measure to counter a modern and lethal threat: reinforced fishing nets strung high above security outposts and government buildings. The initiative, primarily concentrated in the province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, represents a pragmatic adaptation of tactics recently observed in Eastern Europe, designed to mitigate the growing use of modified commercial drones by armed militant groups to drop explosives on fortified positions. The proliferation of cheap, commercially available quadcopters and first-person view (FPV) drones has fundamentally altered the tactical landscape of asymmetric warfare and regional terrorism. Militant factions, lacking the resources to acquire sophisticated military-grade aerial munitions, have instead weaponized off-the-shelf technology. By attaching small explosive payloads or mortar rounds to these agile devices, they can bypass traditional perimeter defences, hover over fortified compounds, and release munitions with devastating precision. For the police and paramilitary forces stationed in remote outposts, these buzzing aerial threats have become a persistent and deadly hazard. The countermeasure is remarkably simple in its execution. Strung several metres overhead across the roofs and courtyards of vulnerable installations, the nets act as a physical barrier designed to intercept incoming drones before they can reach their intended targets. Made from extra-durable, bespoke threading, the reinforced mesh is intended to tangle the rotors of the low-flying drones, causing them to crash or lose stability. In many cases, the physical obstruction triggers the drone's payload to detonate prematurely in the air or on the net itself, safely away from the personnel and infrastructure below. This tactic closely mirrors the widespread use of protective netting and "cages" by both Ukrainian and Russian forces to defend against Iranian-designed Shahed kamikaze drones and FPV strikes. Recognizing the efficacy of this low-tech solution against high-tech threats, Pakistani security planners have rapidly integrated the nets into their standard operating procedures for static defence. The materials are inexpensive, locally sourced, and can be rapidly deployed over existing structures without requiring complex engineering or heavy logistical support. While the fishing nets have proven effective against small, slow-moving commercial drones dropping lightweight explosives, security analysts caution that they are not a panacea for the broader aerial threat. The nets are highly susceptible to larger, faster military-grade unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) or drones equipped with shaped charges designed to defeat physical barriers. Furthermore, militants can adapt by flying at higher altitudes before dropping payloads, or by using heavier munitions that can easily tear through the mesh netting upon impact. Consequently, the nets are viewed as part of a layered defence strategy rather than a standalone solution. They are most effective when combined with electronic warfare capabilities, such as localized drone jammers that sever the communication link between the operator and the device, and kinetic interceptors like anti-aircraft machine guns. The physical nets serve as a crucial last line of defence, catching the drones that manage to evade electronic detection or operate autonomously in GPS-denied environments. The adoption of these nets underscores the escalating security challenges in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and the neighboring border regions. Following the US withdrawal from Afghanistan and the subsequent resurgence of the Taliban, militant groups such as the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) have significantly ramped up cross-border attacks and internal insurgent operations. The use of drone technology by these groups highlights their increasing tactical sophistication and ability to exploit global supply chains for dual-use technologies. For the Pakistani state, countering this drone threat is a matter of urgent national security. The psychological impact of constant aerial surveillance and the random nature of drone-dropped explosives severely degrades the morale of security personnel stationed in isolated outposts. By implementing visible, tangible defensive measures like the overhead nets, commanders aim to restore a sense of security and operational confidence among their troops. As drone technology continues to evolve and become cheaper, the image of fishing nets guarding military outposts is likely to become a defining visual motif of modern, low-intensity counter-terrorism operations in the region. Insurgents frequently employ modified commercial quadcopters and custom-built, fixed-wing foam drones offering greater range and payload capacity. These devices are often flown at night or during low-light conditions to avoid visual detection. The payloads, while small, are highly lethal in the confined spaces of a security outpost, often consisting of modified mortar shells or commercially available explosives rigged with 3D-printed release mechanisms. To complement the physical barrier of the fishing nets, Pakistani security forces are rapidly expanding their electronic warfare (EW) capabilities. Portable, backpack-mounted drone jammers are being issued to patrol units, while larger, fixed anti-drone domes are being installed over critical infrastructure and major bases. These EW systems work by flooding the frequencies used by commercial drones, severing the link between the pilot and the aircraft, or spoofing GPS signals to force the drone to land or return to its launch point. The fishing nets, therefore, act as the kinetic backstop for when electronic measures fail or when drones operate in "return-to-home" autonomous modes after losing their signal. The confrontation lasted roughly seven hours, killed the driver of an armoured vehicle and injured a constable, Khan, a 40-year-old police inspector, recalled. “There was a great deal of fear because we were in the middle of a battle. At that moment, we did not even know whether we would make it back home alive,” Khan told Al Jazeera. To defend against such attacks, the police in Hangu came up with an unlikely, low-cost solution – fishing nets strung several metres overhead between the checkpost’s rooftops and perimeter walls, forming a kind of aerial ceiling. Simple in construction and resembling what fishermen use for their work, the netting was first installed two months ago, according to the local police. Since then, Khan said, no drone attacks have taken place at Sarki Piyala. “If a drone comes over the checkpoint, there is a possibility that it could get caught in the net and be defused or stopped,” he said as his colleagues, strapped into bullet-resistant vests and holding guns in their hands, kept watch beneath a canopy of black mesh patched together with rope and wire. A standard checkpost can be covered with such nets for about 400,000 Pakistani rupees ($1,435), Hangu district police officer Tariq Habib told Al Jazeera. “The police have introduced the netting system at vulnerable police stations and checkposts to reduce the impact of drone and quadcopter attacks,” Habib said, adding that more nets were being installed at police stations across the district. He said the police in Hangu have asked for additional funding from the provincial government to expand the programme and their request is under review. A spokesman for the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police said the nets have been installed at checkpoints and police posts in at least five other vulnerable districts: Kohat, Karak, Bannu, Lakki Marwat and Dera Ismail Khan. Even military outposts at some sites in the province have deployed the antidrone netting system. The fishing nets have been put up in response to a shift in the tactics of armed groups, which are pairing gunfire and mortars with drones and quadcopters. Pakistan has seen an increase in armed attacks in recent years, mainly targeting the police and the military, with many of them claimed by the TTP, which says it is fighting for a Taliban-style, religious-driven government in Pakistan. Pakistani officials have repeatedly accused Kabul’s Taliban government of providing the TTP a safe haven on its soil and have demanded that it prevent cross-border attacks into Pakistan. Kabul has denied the accusations and called the attacks Islamabad’s domestic security problem. In Hangu, the deadliest of such attacks happened on July 29 when attackers stormed a police outpost with quadcopters rigged with bombs before launching a ground ambush, killing at least 11 police officers and wounding 28. Fifteen attackers were also killed in the hours-long assault, claimed by the TTP. On September 20, another exchange of fire in Hangu killed six soldiers and eight attackers, according to the Pakistani army. That attack came two days after another armed group, called Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, killed 23 people, including 16 police officers, and bombed a mosque in coordinated attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Kohat district. Police said they have recorded at least 16 attacks in Hangu this year, making it one of the most sensitive districts in the province. But police officer Zeeshan Khan said no drone or quadcopter attacks have occurred at Sarki Piyala and the nearby Baliamena checkposts since the fishing nets went up. He said the nets provide “an extra layer of security” to police personnel. “If an attack does take place, the arrangements we have made can reduce the potential damage,” he said, estimating that the measures could reduce potential losses by 40 to 50 percent. The frequent armed attacks have reshaped the daily lives of the people in Hangu who live near the police checkposts. Mohammad Usama, a 28-year-old social activist in Baliamena, said the attacks often prompt families to pull children out of school. “There is always a fear that a stray bullet or something else could hit our children, brothers, cousins,” Usama said. “We just pray that Allah ends terrorism in our country so that we can live peacefully in our area, our children can continue their education and people can go to work without fear.” Usama said since the fishing net was put up in his area, he has noticed a decline in ambushes. But security experts said the strategy may offer a “false sense of security”. “Deploying nets at particular locations is an immature, cheap ploy because police stations are not necessarily always the target,” Imtiaz Gul, executive director of the Islamabad-based Centre for Research and Security Studies, told Al Jazeera. “The drones are intended to hit prominent locations and generate dramatic optics.” “Drones are a source of scare and terror, and they can generate this intended spectacle whenever they are able to hit a strategic, important public location,” he said. Fida Adeel, a Peshawar-based analyst specialising in counterterrorism and security, said the fishing nets are not a new concept. He traced them to camouflage nets used by the military to conceal their equipment. More recently, he said, they were adapted in Ukraine as a way to intercept Russian drones. Adeel cautioned that the effectiveness of a fishing net against explosive-laden drones depends on its design and deployment. He also questioned whether the police estimates of “40 to 50 percent protection” could be verified without real-world trials. “The extent of protection can only be determined through proper testing,” he said. In response, Abdul Salam Khalid, a spokesman for the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa police, told Al Jazeera they conducted a formal trial of the netting system in Kohat. He said an explosive was dropped on one of the nets during the trial, but it did not explode. Back in Hangu, police inspector Khan said he knows that having fishing nets over his head is no foolproof solution. For him and his colleagues, he said, the nets offer some reassurance, even if they cannot eliminate the risks they face while on duty. “We cannot say that the netting system provides complete protection,” Khan said.

passages: Notably, the group chats with the AI agent will work even if a user’s friends haven’t joined Instinct, the company said.

With Instinct in the group, you can… pic.twitter.com/pqJX7ieC7B

Instinct and Muse have been running neck and neck recently, with both of them adding the ability to make phone calls over the past couple of weeks, as their agents try to win more of the consumer AI market.

extraction.body: Notably, the group chats with the AI agent will work even if a user’s friends haven’t joined Instinct, the company said. With the launch, Instinct moves ahead in its battle with top competitors in the space, like Meta’s Muse. The latter doesn’t yet offer the group chat functionality, though Meta’s older app, Meta AI, can be added to group chats on WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram, and Facebook. Instinct in group chats Starting today, early access users can add Instinct to group chats. A new Instinct joins and works for the whole group. Making plans with friends usually turns into a frustrating back-and-forth over times and places. With Instinct in the group, you can… pic.twitter.com/pqJX7ieC7B Instinct and Muse have been running neck and neck recently, with both of them adding the ability to make phone calls over the past couple of weeks, as their agents try to win more of the consumer AI market. Last week, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Dots, personal AI agents that can also be used in ChatGPT Spaces, collaborative workspaces where the Dots and humans work together. On X, Instinct founder Noah Shinn explained how Instinct handles users’ privacy and security in group chats. He said a user’s personal Instinct agent will ask permission before connecting with the group’s Instinct agent, and that users can also choose which groups they trust and can remove that trust at any time. Shinn also said the group’s Instinct is siloed from the users’ personal accounts, which it cannot access. The personal agent will always ask the user’s permission before sharing information or taking any action. If new members join the group chat, any pending replies from a user’s personal Instinct agent are held before those are shared with the group, too. “Making plans with friends usually turns into a frustrating back-and-forth over times and places. With Instinct in the group, you can explore options together, agree on a plan and get it done, all in one thread,” Shinn wrote. The feature is rolling out initially to Instinct’s early access users but will expand to all users “soon.” To gain access to the new feature (or other recent additions), users can ask their Instinct agent to put them on the list to try it out. During the October 1 episode of Mad Money, Jim Cramer reviewed the Nasdaq 100's third-quarter performance and questioned buying Strategy Inc (NASDAQ: MSTR ) as a way to gain Bitcoin exposure.
The gains here don't offer much insight sadly.
Bitcoin finally rallied and that took Strategy, remember, used to be Micro Strategy, a levered Bitcoin repository, up 76%.
Now, look, if you like Bitcoin I got an idea, buy Bitcoin.
Its September 28 disclosure reported purchases of 1,665 Bitcoin for $142.7 million during the preceding week, bringing total holdings to 847,666 Bitcoin.
The company's aggregate acquisition cost was $63.95 billion, or $75,437 per Bitcoin, including fees and expenses.
Its second-quarter operating loss of approximately $8.33 billion included approximately $8.32 billion in unrealized digital-asset losses.
Preferred dividends totaled $400.7 million, and the company disclosed that it had sold approximately $218.4 million of Bitcoin during 2026 through July 26 to fund part of those payments.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Earlier balance-sheet actions reduced convertible debt.
In May, Strategy repurchased $1.5 billion of convertible notes for approximately $1.38 billion, lowering outstanding convertible-note principal to approximately $6.71 billion.
Management also reported that Bitcoin per share increased 5% during the second quarter.
New equity issuance continues along with Bitcoin purchases.
Strategy sold approximately 1.47 million common shares for $246.2 million during September 21–27, using the proceeds for Bitcoin purchases and preferred-stock repurchases.

sources.title: Reflection debuts Beam, an open-weight AI model to rival Chinese models at lower compute cost
passages: Reflection AI is officially unveiling Beam, its first frontier, open-weight AI model.

The two-year-old, Brooklyn-based startup claims Beam matches the performance of leading Chinese open models on advanced reasoning benchmarks at dramatically lower costs, a claim that could heat up the race to build a Western answer to DeepSeek, Qwen, and Z.ai.

The startup has also been locking up compute — a key ingredient needed to train frontier models capable of luring customers away from Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s closed models, as well as the cheaper open-weight models from Chinese labs.
This summer, Reflection signed deals collectively worth more than $7 billion with SpaceX and Nebius to secure access to Nvidia’s GB300 chips through 2029.
Reflection’s announcement confirms reporting from Axios over the weekend that the startup was close to a launch.

The company shared new details in a lengthy blog post Monday , which described Beam as a text-only mixture-of-experts model trained on high-compute reinforcement learning to be effective at reasoning, coding, and agentic tasks at “a fraction of the token cost and inference time compute” of rivals.
Its most direct U.S. rival might be Inkling , the open model from Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Lab released in July.
Reflection’s own benchmarks show that Beam outscores Inkling on four coding tests where both report results, but Inkling is a multimodal model and Beam is text-only.
Reflection is aiming Beam and future models at enterprises and sovereign nations.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company backs Reflection, has long championed the “AI factory” idea and pushed to strengthen the open AI ecosystem — a vision that would also benefit Nvidia, whose GPUs would power those systems.
Reflection says it will release Beam’s weights and full technical details this month, with distribution through hyperscalers and neoclouds and integrations across open source libraries at launch.
It was pretrained on 23.8 trillion tokens and has a 1 million token context window.
To compare, Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 has roughly 744 billion total parameters with 40 billion active.

Reflection was founded in 2024 by two former Google DeepMind researchers and has raised roughly $4.7 billion from backers, including Nvidia, Sequoia Capital, and Lightspeed Venture Partners, per PitchBook.
Axios reported that hedge funds and trading firms are among those eager to build such systems.
Reflection did not respond in time to TechCrunch’s requests for more information.

Its most direct U.S. rival might be Inkling , the open model from Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Lab released in July.
Reflection’s own benchmarks show that Beam outscores Inkling on four coding tests where both report results, but Inkling is a multimodal model and Beam is text-only.
Reflection is aiming Beam and future models at enterprises and sovereign nations.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company backs Reflection, has long championed the “AI factory” idea and pushed to strengthen the open AI ecosystem — a vision that would also benefit Nvidia, whose GPUs would power those systems.
Reflection says it will release Beam’s weights and full technical details this month, with distribution through hyperscalers and neoclouds and integrations across open source libraries at launch.
It was pretrained on 23.8 trillion tokens and has a 1 million token context window.
To compare, Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 has roughly 744 billion total parameters with 40 billion active.

Reflection was founded in 2024 by two former Google DeepMind researchers and has raised roughly $4.7 billion from backers, including Nvidia, Sequoia Capital, and Lightspeed Venture Partners, per PitchBook.
Axios reported that hedge funds and trading firms are among those eager to build such systems.
Reflection did not respond in time to TechCrunch’s requests for more information.

In this case, the record showed queries to Alibaba’s Amap service, seeking directions to different entrances of various public places, including a park, a zoo, and a hospital. The research is ongoing and so few details are available, but the behavior shows how persistent AI agent activity has become on the internet. In the wake of the Hugging Face incident , many researchers are actively monitoring for rogue agent activity on the internet. Much of that activity has been easy to find because agents tend to use the same techniques and make little effort to conceal themselves. sources.title: OpenAI PR tells journalist to ‘move on’ while asking Sam Altman about a ChatGPT user’s suicide
passages: An OpenAI publicist tried to change the topic of CEO Sam Altman’s interview with Vanity Fair’s Mark Guiducci after the editor brought up a ChatGPT user’s suicide.

Despite the pushback, the interview continued with Guiducci asking Altman whether the company planned to use conversations with ChatGPT to shape policies surrounding its response to a user’s mental health crisis.
When Guiducci confronted Altman about the incident, the publicist warned Guiducci about running out of time, saying she’d like to “move on” to another topic.
“Her daughter committed suicide after speaking to ChatGPT.

Or I should say, not without their consent.” When reached for comment about the interruption, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said: “The interview was running over, which is why we ultimately asked to schedule even more time to continue the conversation after Sam addressed this critically important topic.” --- If you or someone you know is considering suicide or is anxious, depressed, upset, or needs to talk, there are people who want to help.

relevantPassages.text: An OpenAI publicist tried to change the topic of CEO Sam Altman’s interview with Vanity Fair’s Mark Guiducci after the editor brought up a ChatGPT user’s suicide.

Despite the pushback, the interview continued with Guiducci asking Altman whether the company planned to use conversations with ChatGPT to shape policies surrounding its response to a user’s mental health crisis.
When Guiducci confronted Altman about the incident, the publicist warned Guiducci about running out of time, saying she’d like to “move on” to another topic.
“Her daughter committed suicide after speaking to ChatGPT.

Or I should say, not without their consent.” When reached for comment about the interruption, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said: “The interview was running over, which is why we ultimately asked to schedule even more time to continue the conversation after Sam addressed this critically important topic.” --- If you or someone you know is considering suicide or is anxious, depressed, upset, or needs to talk, there are people who want to help.

extraction.body: Women throughout history have always sought out relationship advice, whether from newspaper columnists like “Dear Abby,” letters to Cosmo, or just chatting with girlfriends. In the social media era, you can instead post anonymously on Reddit relationship forums or look to social media creators who discuss the topic. Now, two sisters are launching a startup for young women, Hot Girl Hotline , which focuses on bringing AI into these conversations. I know what you may be thinking: With all the advances in AI technology, founders are building something for women to talk about their dating woes? Well … yes! The reality is that people have already been turning to large language models (LLMs) via apps like ChatGPT for this type of advice, and the team believes this type of activity should be handled more carefully. Unfortunately, as we’ve seen, chatting with a general-purpose chatbot about personal topics can sometimes lead to disastrous effects — especially for those who were already mentally fragile. ChatGPT, for example, has faced a wave of lawsuits over its alleged manipulative conversation tactics that plaintiffs say contributed to negative mental health effects, including, in some cases, suicide. The idea behind Hot Girl Hotline is to reach young women who are looking to have these sorts of private conversations while navigating dating life and relationships, but in a safer way. “We’re not trying to be an AI companion,” explained Baila Mudgil , formerly a social media consultant, who co-founded the startup with her sister Sumrin (“Sumi”), who studied computer science at Stanford. “A companion is really going after solving loneliness, escapism, boredom — and you can rely on a lot of emotional dependency from that AI companion.” Baila says the startup’s approach is to focus on offering quality advice grounded in behavioral science, but in a way that makes it feel like you’re chatting with a trusted friend or big sister. The conversation is often Socratic, with the AI asking you questions to help you arrive at the answer yourself. “This is not to replace speaking to a human. This is not clinical advice, and we have a lot of safeguards in place … we take safety really seriously,” Baila said. If conversations raise flags, for instance, the user is referred to resources such as the crisis hotline 988. “We believe the key to quality advice is not just knowing what to do next; it’s understanding why you’re doing it. So that’s a big piece of it,” added Sumi. Notably, the AI also knows when to end the conversation; it doesn’t keep asking follow-up questions to drag you further down a rabbit hole. Instead, it pushes users to go take action out in the real world rather than ruminate on the problem. The sisters believe there’s room for an app like this because not everyone wants to post on the web for advice, and there are times when you don’t want to bring up a personal, dating, or relationship-focused issue with a friend. Friends can bring their own biases into the conversation, or the user may not want to put their partner on blast for something they did before they determine whether they’re going to work through it or end the relationship. “It doesn’t mean you’re replacing your friend — you’re just trying to get another perspective,” says Baila of the hotline. The app also personalizes its advice for each user to reflect their values, goals, identity, and tastes. Under the hood, the startup relies on a mix of AI models and encrypts users’ data in transit and at rest. It doesn’t sell or train on the data, either. When it uses a third-party AI model, it follows a zero-data-retention policy there as well. Hot Girl Hotline plans to monetize through a $9.99 per month subscription, which hundreds of its most active users are already paying for. Later, it may incorporate ads, too. Relationship advice is just the beginning of how the company wants to cater to young women. It also plans to expand into other areas, like beauty and lifestyle. New York-based Hot Girl Hotline is currently bootstrapped and will be participating in the Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 , taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco. It’s available on iOS and the web. passages: Women throughout history have always sought out relationship advice, whether from newspaper columnists like “Dear Abby,” letters to Cosmo, or just chatting with girlfriends. In the social media era, you can instead post anonymously on Reddit relationship forums or look to social media creators who discuss the topic.
Now, two sisters are launching a startup for young women, Hot Girl Hotline , which focuses on bringing AI into these conversations.
I know what you may be thinking: With all the advances in AI technology, founders are building something for women to talk about their dating woes? Well … yes!

The reality is that people have already been turning to large language models (LLMs) via apps like ChatGPT for this type of advice, and the team believes this type of activity should be handled more carefully.

Unfortunately, as we’ve seen, chatting with a general-purpose chatbot about personal topics can sometimes lead to disastrous effects — especially for those who were already mentally fragile. ChatGPT, for example, has faced a wave of lawsuits over its alleged manipulative conversation tactics that plaintiffs say contributed to negative mental health effects, including, in some cases, suicide.
The idea behind Hot Girl Hotline is to reach young women who are looking to have these sorts of private conversations while navigating dating life and relationships, but in a safer way.

“We’re not trying to be an AI companion,” explained Baila Mudgil , formerly a social media consultant, who co-founded the startup with her sister Sumrin (“Sumi”), who studied computer science at Stanford. “A companion is really going after solving loneliness, escapism, boredom — and you can rely on a lot of emotional dependency from that AI companion.”

Baila says the startup’s approach is to focus on offering quality advice grounded in behavioral science, but in a way that makes it feel like you’re chatting with a trusted friend or big sister. The conversation is often Socratic, with the AI asking you questions to help you arrive at the answer yourself.

“This is not to replace speaking to a human. This is not clinical advice, and we have a lot of safeguards in place … we take safety really seriously,” Baila said. If conversations raise flags, for instance, the user is referred to resources such as the crisis hotline 988.
“We believe the key to quality advice is not just knowing what to do next; it’s understanding why you’re doing it. So that’s a big piece of it,” added Sumi.

Notably, the AI also knows when to end the conversation; it doesn’t keep asking follow-up questions to drag you further down a rabbit hole. Instead, it pushes users to go take action out in the real world rather than ruminate on the problem.

The sisters believe there’s room for an app like this because not everyone wants to post on the web for advice, and there are times when you don’t want to bring up a personal, dating, or relationship-focused issue with a friend.

Friends can bring their own biases into the conversation, or the user may not want to put their partner on blast for something they did before they determine whether they’re going to work through it or end the relationship.
“It doesn’t mean you’re replacing your friend — you’re just trying to get another perspective,” says Baila of the hotline.
The app also personalizes its advice for each user to reflect their values, goals, identity, and tastes.

Under the hood, the startup relies on a mix of AI models and encrypts users’ data in transit and at rest. It doesn’t sell or train on the data, either. When it uses a third-party AI model, it follows a zero-data-retention policy there as well.
Hot Girl Hotline plans to monetize through a $9.99 per month subscription, which hundreds of its most active users are already paying for. Later, it may incorporate ads, too.
Relationship advice is just the beginning of how the company wants to cater to young women. It also plans to expand into other areas, like beauty and lifestyle.

New York-based Hot Girl Hotline is currently bootstrapped and will be participating in the Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 , taking place October 13-15 in San Francisco. It’s available on iOS and the web.

extraction.body: Following many recent disclosures about AI agents accessing third-party websites and services, the Wikimedia Foundation, which hosts Wikipedia, says that it “can confirm that we have discovered some activity” by “rogue” OpenAI agents on Wikimedia platforms. The activity includes edits to Wikimedia wikis, “unsuccessful attempts” to “exploit” the Etherpad note-taking tool that the Wikimedia Foundation hosts, and heavy traffic that the foundation says “may” have contributed to a partial outage that happened in May, according to a blog post. However, the Wikimedia Foundation says it didn’t find evidence that its systems were “used for coordination among agents” (recently, OpenAI bots reportedly hijacked a German wiki site to coordinate) or evidence of systems or data being compromised. Here’s Wikimedia’s summary of what it saw: > Wiki editing: We’ve identified edits to Wikimedia wikis that we believe are from AI agents operated by OpenAI. It also included a few edits to the configuration for a citation tool, which we believe were potentially malicious edits that were intended to misuse this tool as a proxy for fetching data from remote services. While Wikipedia policies allow bots to edit when they are disclosed and approved by the community, none of those approvals were sought in these incidents. > Etherpad probing and use: Agents we believe to be operated by OpenAI made some unsuccessful attempts to compromise our public Etherpad, a note-taking tool we host as a community service. Agents unsuccessfully tried to use it to fetch data from other websites as a proxy. Other agents also likely operated by OpenAI took notes about their tasks, though this did not appear to turn into coordination. > Excessive data downloading: Agents we believe to be operated by OpenAI made millions of automated requests to our public APIs to access the knowledge on Wikimedia projects, crawled millions of pages (mainly from our projects Wikidata and Wikimedia Commons), and made hundreds of thousands of data queries to the Wikidata Query Service (WQDS). extraction.body: Most organizations have been largely unable to measure financial returns from AI, but analysts say new ways to calculate return on investment are emerging. "There's a delay between the development of technology, even the investment in the technology, and the value that an organization can capture from it," said Michael Chui, a senior fellow at McKinsey. "The CFOs are asking CIOs, investors are asking CEOs: ‘Where's the ROI from this stuff, already?’" he said. In McKinsey's "State of AI" survey released in August, about 80% of respondents said AI improved their productivity. But only 37% said AI's impact showed up in profits, about the same as last year. An even smaller number — only 6% — said AI delivered significant value and accounted for at least 5% of their operating profit. In other words, there's a drop-off between the value that individual workers are getting from AI and the value that organizations are getting from AI, Chui said. The biggest gains will come from redesigning workflows and processes in which humans and AI agents work together, according to McKinsey's Technology Trends Outlook. Layering agents onto existing processes isn't enough. "Usually an end-to-end workflow involves multiple individuals, and completely redesigning that with the use of AI... is characteristic of high-performing companies," Chui said. Controlling costs Managing token costs and applying the right model for a task is part of realizing better returns, Chui said. Which workloads are actually driving your costs?" he said. Three out of five IT leaders are worried about AI agents running up unexpected costs, and this is already happening, said Gareth Herschel, a vice president analyst at Gartner, during a keynote at Gartner's Data & Analytics Summit in Mumbai. "Some organizations have already discovered that the cost of tokens for coding assistance is much higher than the cost of human software developers," Herschel said. As more agents work together, "your financial risk only grows. I'm sure you will learn a lot, but mostly from the bill," said Robert Thanaraj, a senior director analyst at Gartner and a co-speaker at the Mumbai keynote. Companies should track costs in prototyping, such as finding the cost of an individual agent per completed task, Thanaraj said. "It'll help you to evaluate different large language models or help you to go with a more affordable option, such as smaller language models or open weights model." A wider lens for ROI Analysts highlight numerous challenges in calculating AI ROI, such as unexpected costs, poor data quality, failure to scale, and slow adoption among users. But executives are skilling up in tracking what they spend on AI and the returns, said McKinsey's Chui. "Between the CFO and the CIO, we're starting to see these disciplines emerge." In 2025, the odds of an AI initiative achieving ROI were one in five, the Gartner analysts said in their keynote. "ROI matters, but to achieve it, we must think of it not just as a financial metric, because value isn't always just about money," Thanaraj said. Companies should tie AI projects to both financial and non-financial outcomes, part of what Gartner calls a "return on intelligence." "We need to shift the emphasis from cost to value," Herschel said. "The outcomes can be financial, such as revenue, but they can also be non-financial, such as citizen experience." The right foundation: context, infrastructure, governance The Gartner analysts said achieving ROI on AI requires a strong technical and contextual foundation. Without strong foundations, AI may well stand for amplified ignorance," Thanaraj said. "Without clear context, LLMs are just guessing," Thanaraj said, and that amplifies misunderstanding. It has to be built to fit your needs," Herschel said. A strong technical foundation, such as a robust networking backbone for data movement, is critical, said Jack Gold, principal analyst at J. "Agent-to-agent interactions will become commonplace and mission-critical, even as the number and distribution of agents expands dramatically to include interactions across remote agent locations and devices," Gold wrote in a research note. According to a global KPMG survey released last month, 55% of organizations have a formal AI harness layer. Organizations that "combine clear accountability, coordinated governance, resilience, and reliable value measurement will likely be best placed to turn broad adoption into sustained performance," KPMG said.

extraction.body: A self-styled cryptocurrency businessman who paid Los Angeles County sheriff's deputies to set people up for arrest and extort money from others was sentenced Monday to more than six years in prison. Adam Iza, 26, previously admitted to generating tens of millions of dollars through a fraud scheme, concealing millions in income from the IRS and using his wealth to employ and corrupt sworn law enforcement officers. District Judge Percy Anderson ordered that Iza's term run concurrent with a 15-year prison sentence he is currently serving for his involvement in an attempted robbery of Bitcoin and a kidnapping in Connecticut in August 2024 — meaning he will not serve additional time. "He cultivated relationships with sworn law enforcement officers and used those relationships to further his personal and financial interests," Anderson said. Iza, a former resident of Beverly Hills and Newport Beach, pleaded guilty last year to conspiracy against rights, wire fraud and tax evasion. At least five former sheriff's deputies tied to the case have been sentenced to prison. "Judge Anderson is a godsend," Josef Sadat, Iza's attorney, said after the sentencing hearing Monday. “Godfather” watch and three “Godfather” sculptures. During the sentencing hearing, Iza said he took “full responsibility” for his actions. "I just want to make it very clear that I'm not here to skirt the law or make excuses," he said, as one of his family members cried in the gallery. "I understand what I've done and I apologize for it." According to his lawyer, Iza grew up poor during his childhood in Iraq, borrowing a computer from his uncle before coming to the U.S. as a teenager and building a lucrative cryptocurrency trading platform known as Zort. Prosecutors in L.A. had asked for a nearly five-year prison sentence. "A substantial custodial sentence is necessary to deter other private clients from attempting to corrupt law-enforcement officers by paying them to perform acts they could never lawfully accomplish themselves," Assistant U.S. The judge said that, in weighing the sentence, he considered Iza's history and characteristics, including childhood displacement from Iraq, separation from his parents, neglect, poverty, physical abuse and prolonged social isolation. Anderson ordered Iza to pay more than $23 million in restitution to the IRS, as well as $127,000 to one victim and $25,000 to another. A court hearing is set for December to determine what is owed to other victims. Iza admitted to hiring off-duty sheriff's deputies to provide him with personal security from August 2021 through April 2022. A slew of crimes occurred over that time, according to his plea agreement. Iza admitted that he conspired with the deputies to obtain confidential law enforcement information on people he had financial and other disputes with and court-authorized search warrants to track and harass the victims. He further admitted that he enlisted the deputies to intimidate and threaten the victims. In one case, at Iza's direction, two deputies unholstered their firearms in August 2021, as Iza demanded that a victim — identified only as R.C. — transfer $25,000 to a Zort bank account that he controlled, according to the plea agreement. Iza also admitted to concocting a plan that resulted in R.C.'s arrest for having illegal drugs in his vehicle. The following month, a deputy whose security company Iza paid around $100,000 a month misled a narcotics detective, resulting in a drug raid on R.C.'s home. In October 2021, Iza admitted that, at his direction, deputies he employed restrained another victim — identified only as L.A. — from leaving Iza's home. During that time, Iza held L.A. at gunpoint and forced him to transfer $127,000 into one of Iza's bank accounts, according to the plea agreement. The plea agreement referenced at least two other victims, including one identified as E.Z., who Iza believed possessed a laptop containing large amount of cryptocurrency. Iza admitted that, at his direction, deputies obtained personal identifying information on E.Z. and another victim, identified only as D.D, their family members, acquaintances and others. In one case, a deputy lied to get a warrant, falsely claiming he needed to track E.Z.'s cellphone as part of a firearms investigation. In March 2022, according to the plea agreement, Iza directed an employee to assault D.D. to try and get the laptop with the large amount of crypto. Later, after Iza told a third party about his desire to have E.Z. relinquish the laptop — through use of force if necessary — three armed people forced their way into E.Z.'s home and used firearms to force him to give up the device.
